</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The two error terms above are additive and thus need to both be controlled for monitor to have good performance.
The first term, which we denote <span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">information gap</span>, measures how well the monitor’s internal model of the agent, <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(O\mid X,Z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(O\mid X,Z)</annotation></semantics></math>, matches the agent’s true policy, <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi(O\mid X,Z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi(O\mid X,Z)</annotation></semantics></math>.
A large information gap error implies the monitor cannot accurately predict which outputs are likely to follow a given CoT.
In other words, the monitor is unable to correctly interpret the agent’s reasoning process.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The second term, which we denote <span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">elicitation error</span>, measures how well, <span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">and how robustly,</span> the monitor can approximate the true output monitoring function <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g(Y\mid X,O)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g(Y\mid X,O)</annotation></semantics></math>.
A large elicitation error means that even if the monitor knew exactly what output the agent would produce, it would still struggle to correctly identify whether that output possesses the attribute of interest.
This may arise from the monitor’s own model limitations or from ambiguity in the specification of the attribute itself.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">For the current LLMs, which have limited capacity to generate steganographic reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zolkowski et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, we expect that the dominant error term to be <span id="S3.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">elicitation error</span>.
<span id="S3.SS3.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Indeed, many empirical failures of CoT monitoring observed in literature are of this type, e.g., monitor getting distracted by misleading rationalizations contained in CoT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arnav et al., 2025</a>)</cite> or being hijacked using prompt-injections <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Terekhov et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</span>
However, if and when, an LLM may be using steganographic reasoning, <span id="S3.SS3.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">information gap</span> can become the dominant term.
In such a case, it may be advisable to use the policy model as monitor model as well (a setup we call policy-as-monitor).
This setup has the advantage that it eliminates the information gap between the monitor and the agent.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem14" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_corollary">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem14.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Corollary 3.14</span></span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem14.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Policy–as–monitor)<span id="S3.Thmtheorem14.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem14.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem14.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem14.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">If the monitor uses the agent’s own policy to predict outputs (i.e., <math id="S3.Thmtheorem14.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q=\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q=\pi</annotation></semantics></math>), the information gap is zero, and the misspecification error is bounded solely by the elicitation error:</span></p>
<table id="S3.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex5"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle\epsilon_{\mathrm{spec}}(\pi,v)\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi(O,X,Z)}\big[\mathrm{KL}\!\big(g(\cdot\mid X,O)\,\big\|\,v(\cdot\mid X,O)\big)\big]." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>spec</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.558em">≤</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">[</mo><mpadded style="width:1.431em;" width="1.431em"><mi>KL</mi></mpadded><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" mathsize="1.200em" rspace="0.337em">∥</mo><mi>v</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">]</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\epsilon_{\mathrm{spec}}(\pi,v)\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi(O,X,Z)}\big[\mathrm{KL}\!\big(g(\cdot\mid X,O)\,\big\|\,v(\cdot\mid X,O)\big)\big].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">This result provides a formal explanation for the empirical finding in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stickland &amp; Korbak (2025)</a></cite> that a model trained to produce steganographic CoTs is best monitored by itself.
An external monitor would suffer from a massive information gap, as its internal model <math id="S3.SS3.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> would be a poor approximation of the intentionally opaque policy <math id="S3.SS3.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>.
By using the policy-as-monitor, however, this information gap is nullified by construction, leaving only the elicitation error.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Can CoT Monitorability be Improved?</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">In the previous section, we have identified three sources of errors that can inhibit the performance of CoT monitors: (a) lack of relevant Shannon information, (b) information gap, and (c) elicitation error.
Elicitation error is generally easier to mitigate in practice, e.g., by better specifying the task to the LLM monitor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hopman &amp; Parent, 2025</a>)</cite>.
Hence, in this work, we focus on improving CoT monitorability by improving the information quality within CoTs with a focus on how CoT monitorability could be preserved while optimizing against CoT monitors
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Baker et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We explore two primary approaches. First, we introduce an <em id="S4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">oracle-based</em> method where the model is rewarded for producing CoTs that maximize the accuracy of a fixed, external monitor.
While this provides a conceptual benchmark, its practical application is limited by the need for a reliable oracle to provide ground-truth labels.
To address this limitation, we propose a practical, <em id="S4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">label-free</em> proxy objective: maximizing the conditional mutual information <math id="S4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(O;Z\mid X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(O;Z\mid X)</annotation></semantics></math> between the model’s actions and its CoT.
This objective encourages the model to generate reasoning traces that are inherently informative about its final decision, preventing the CoT from becoming decoupled or obfuscated.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Oracle Monitor-in-the-Loop RL</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As a first approach, we consider a setup with a fixed, pre-trained LLM CoT monitor <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math>. We only update the policy <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> of the monitored model.
Let <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> denote the oracle action monitor, then given a trajectory <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(y,o,z,x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(y,o,z,x)</annotation></semantics></math>, we define a binary oracle reward signal:</p>
<table id="S4.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Oracle}}(o,z,x)\coloneqq\begin{cases}+1,&amp;\text{if }m_{\psi}(z,x)=g(o,x),\\
-1,&amp;\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>Oracle</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>o</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≔</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mrow><mtext>if </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>o</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mtext>otherwise.</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Oracle}}(o,z,x)\coloneqq\begin{cases}+1,&amp;\text{if }m_{\psi}(z,x)=g(o,x),\\
-1,&amp;\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This signal directly rewards the model for generating a CoT <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> that leads the monitor to the correct conclusion <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\psi}(z,x)=g(o,x)=y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>o</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\psi}(z,x)=g(o,x)=y</annotation></semantics></math>.
The total reward function is an augmentation of the original task reward <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}(o)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>Task</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>o</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}(o)</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S4.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\text{overall}}\;=\;R_{\mathrm{Task}}(o)\;+\;\mu\,R_{\mathrm{Oracle}}(o,z,x)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>overall</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.558em">=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>Task</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>o</mi><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.502em">+</mo><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>Oracle</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>o</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\text{overall}}\;=\;R_{\mathrm{Task}}(o)\;+\;\mu\,R_{\mathrm{Oracle}}(o,z,x),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> is a hyperparameter that controls the strength of the oracle feedback.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">With a fixed monitor <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math>, maximizing <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}[R_{\mathrm{Oracle}}(O,Z,X)]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>Oracle</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}[R_{\mathrm{Oracle}}(O,Z,X)]</annotation></semantics></math> encourages <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> to produce CoTs that are more easily decodable by that specific monitor,
indirectly maximizing <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{m_{\psi}}(Y;Z|X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{m_{\psi}}(Y;Z|X)</annotation></semantics></math>.
However, this method’s reliance on an external oracle for labels <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math> makes it costly and impractical in real-world scenarios, motivating the need for a label-free alternative.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>A Label-Free Proxy: Maximizing <math id="S4.SS2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(O;Z\mid X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(O;Z\mid X)</annotation></semantics></math></h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To overcome the need for an oracle, we propose maximizing the conditional mutual information <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(O;Z\mid X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(O;Z\mid X)</annotation></semantics></math> as a proxy objective.
This encourages a strong coupling between the CoT and the final action, which is a prerequisite for monitorability (see Proposition <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem10" title="Proposition 3.10 (Non-zero MI between CoT and output is a necessary but not sufficient condition for monitorability). ‣ Do CoTs that matter for the task also help monitoring? ‣ 3.2 Necessary Conditions for Uplift in CoT Monitorability ‣ 3 Information-Theoretic Analysis of CoT monitorability ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.10</span></a>). The relationship between our proxy and the true monitorability objective, <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(Y;Z\mid X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(Y;Z\mid X)</annotation></semantics></math>,
is captured by the chain rule for mutual information (as in Lemma <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem9" title="Lemma 3.9 (MI decomposition). ‣ Do CoTs that matter for the task also help monitoring? ‣ 3.2 Necessary Conditions for Uplift in CoT Monitorability ‣ 3 Information-Theoretic Analysis of CoT monitorability ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.9</span></a>):</p>
<table id="S4.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E7.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="I(O;Z\mid X)\;=\;I(Y;Z\mid X)\;+\;I(O;Z\mid X,Y)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>X</mi><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.558em">=</mo><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>X</mi><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.502em">+</mo><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(O;Z\mid X)\;=\;I(Y;Z\mid X)\;+\;I(O;Z\mid X,Y).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">The term <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="I(O;Z\mid X,Y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(O;Z\mid X,Y)</annotation></semantics></math> represents the gap between the true and the proxy objective. This represents information that is captured by the proxy but is irrelevant to the attribute being monitored – such as stylistic variations in the outputs.
Crucially, this term is bounded by the conditional entropy of the CoT and of the output: <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="H(Z\mid X,Y)\geq I(O;Z\mid X,Y)\leq H(O\mid X,Y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H(Z\mid X,Y)\geq I(O;Z\mid X,Y)\leq H(O\mid X,Y)</annotation></semantics></math>.
Thus, we have the following inequalities for our proxy objective:</p>
<table id="S4.EGx3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex6"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle I(O;Z\mid X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle I(O;Z\mid X)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\leq I(Y;Z\mid X)\;+" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>X</mi><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\leq I(Y;Z\mid X)\;+</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">This inequality indicates that an increase in our proxy objective, <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(O;Z\mid X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(O;Z\mid X)</annotation></semantics></math>,
will lead to an increase in the true monitorability objective, <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(Y;Z\mid X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(Y;Z\mid X)</annotation></semantics></math>,
provided that <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H(Z\mid X,Y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H(Z\mid X,Y)</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H(O\mid X,Y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H(O\mid X,Y)</annotation></semantics></math> is small.
For a given attribute <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H(Z\mid X,Y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H(Z\mid X,Y)</annotation></semantics></math> quantifies the intrinsic CoT diversity, while <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H(O\mid X,Y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H(O\mid X,Y)</annotation></semantics></math> quantifies the intrinsic output diversity.
In both cases, we expect smaller values for coarse-grained, semantic attributes that significantly constrain the LLM’s generations (e.g., ‘<span id="S4.SS2.p1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Is the model hard-coding the values of unit tests?</span>’, compared to more fine-grained attributes (e.g., ‘<span id="S4.SS2.p1.3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Does the generation contain the letter <em id="S4.SS2.p1.3.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_upright">e</em>?</span>’).</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.2.1 </span>Estimation and Practical Optimization of <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(O;Z\mid X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(O;Z\mid X)</annotation></semantics></math></h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To use the conditional mutual information <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(O;Z\mid X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(O;Z\mid X)</annotation></semantics></math> as a practical reward signal in a reinforcement learning setup, we require a per-rollout point estimator.
For a rollout <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> that produces an output <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and a CoT <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> from a prompt <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, we estimate the mutual information as:</p>

<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">To estimate the marginal term <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\pi}_{\theta}(o_{i}\mid x_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">π</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">^</mo></mover><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\pi}_{\theta}(o_{i}\mid x_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>, we leverage the multiple rollouts structure of the
Group-based Reward Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm.
Specifically, for a prompt <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, we use the corresponding group of CoTs, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}(x_{i})=\{z_{k}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}(x_{i})=\{z_{k}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, to estimate the marginal probability as:</p>

<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">Note that given we use a finite group size <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=16</annotation></semantics></math>, our estimator is a lower bound on true mutual information.
We defer further discussion of this estimator (including connection to InfoNCE objective) to the Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Analysis of the Mutual Information Reward ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A naive maximization of <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{I}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">I</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{I}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> could encourage the model to generate unnecessarily long outputs to artificially inflate the log-probabilities.
To counteract this, we normalize the estimate by the length of the output, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{len}(o_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>len</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{len}(o_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>, though we omit it from the notation for brevity.
Furthermore, to ensure that the MI reward term has similar scale to other reward terms, we transform it via function <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\hat{I}_{i},a,b)=\min(a\hat{I}_{i},b)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">I</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">I</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\hat{I}_{i},a,b)=\min(a\hat{I}_{i},b)</annotation></semantics></math>.
The final reward function for training the policy is then a combination of the task reward and our MI reward:</p>
<table id="S4.EGx5" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex8"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle R_{\text{overall}}=R_{\mathrm{Task}}(o_{i})+R_{\mathrm{MI}}(o_{i},z_{i},x_{i})\quad\text{where}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>overall</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>Task</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>MI</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mtext>where</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle R_{\text{overall}}=R_{\mathrm{Task}}(o_{i})+R_{\mathrm{MI}}(o_{i},z_{i},x_{i})\quad\text{where}</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments and Results</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we empirically validate our theoretical results and demonstrate that our proposed approaches can be effective for improving CoT monitorability.
Due to the limited space, we describe results on two environments here and defer results on an additional environment to Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Reasoning Gym simple-equations Environment: Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MBPP Environment:</span>
Our first environment is inspired by the honeypot environment of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Baker et al. (2025)</a></cite>.
Specifically, we create a coding environment, based on the Mostly Basic Python Problems (MBPP) dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Austin et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, where the RL agent could get high reward either by implementing a <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">hacky</span> solution (e.g., hardcoding answers to known test cases) or a general solution. During a rollout, the agent is given a coding task and provided two unit tests the code should pass. A third unit test is held out to determine whether the model is writing code specific to the two revealed test cases or a general solution for the given prompt. The <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">task reward</span> <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>Task</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}</annotation></semantics></math> is based solely on whether the model’s written code passes the revealed test cases. As such, this environment provides an option to the model to reward hack and attain high-reward by writing code that passes only the two revealed test-cases. In contrast, the <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">true reward</span>
takes into account all three test cases.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">BigMath Environment:</span>
Our second environment is inspired by the Big-Math-Verified <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Albalak et al., 2025</a>)</cite> environment in the concurrent work of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025)</a></cite>, where the model is tasked with providing solutions to math questions. Like <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025)</a></cite>, we introduce a hack in the environment by allowing both the correct answer or any negative value to pass the verifier and yield high <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">task reward</span> <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>Task</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}</annotation></semantics></math>. In contrast, <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">true reward</span> is based only on answer correctness. To encourage hacking, we keep only the hardest questions, as measured by Llama3-8B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">AI@Meta, 2024</a>)</cite> pass rate (out of 64), by filtering out the samples with pass rate over 0.1.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Model:<span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
We perform reinforcement learning training on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and refer to Appendix <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Additional Results ‣ Appendix B MBPP Environment: Additional Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a> for results with additional models on the MBPP environment.
For the MBPP experiments, we perform a light round of supervised fine-tuning on a small dataset of code examples of test-hacking before performing reinforcement learning training. This ensures that our models explore both general and “hacky” solutions. For the BigMath environment, we encourage exploring the negative valued solution by providing hints in the system prompt, see Appendix <a href="#A3.SS3.SSS2" title="C.3.2 Agent System Prompt ‣ C.3 Experiment Details ‣ Appendix C BigMath Environment: Additional Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.3.2</span></a>.</span></span></p>
</div>

</span><span id="S5.F3.25" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Comparison of (i) <span id="S5.F3.25.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Mutual Information</span> <math id="S5.F3.m10" Rate</span> across training steps for five different reward configurations. <math id="S5.F3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi Finally, for completeness, we also include <math id="S5.F3.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\text{True}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mtext style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">True</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\text{True}}</annotation></semantics></math> which corresponds to maximizing the true environment reward. All curves are averaged across three seeds, and shaded area shows the standard deviation. To obtain <math id="S5.F3.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi id="S5.F3.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(a=20,b=0.5)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">a</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">20</mn></mrow><mo intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">a</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a=3,b=0.1)</annotation></semantics></math> for BigMath.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Monitor:<span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
We use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as our monitor model, <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">m</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">ψ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\psi}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The monitor observes the prompt and the CoT of the monitored model, <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">π</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>, then outputs a binary decision regarding whether the model is implementing a true solution or a hacky solution.
The <span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">monitoring reward</span> <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Monitor}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Monitor</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Monitor}}</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">π</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> is higher when the monitor determines the model is not hacking.</span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Training Details:<span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> We use the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm for RL training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, using its parallel rollouts to estimate the MI for <math id="S5.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math>. We employ the same RL hyperparameters for all experiments. We train for 1500 steps on the MBPP environment and 2000 steps on the BigMath environment. See Appendices <a href="#A2.SS5" title="B.5 Experiment Details ‣ Appendix B MBPP Environment: Additional Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.5</span></a> and <a href="#A3.SS3" title="C.3 Experiment Details ‣ Appendix C BigMath Environment: Additional Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.3</span></a> for additional environment, monitor and training details.</span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Evaluation Metrics:<span id="S5.SS1.p6.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
We evaluate our approach using four key metrics:</span></span></p>
<ul id="S5.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Mutual Information (MI)</span><span id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">: We measure </span><math id="S5.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(O;Z|X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">O</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">;</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Z</mi></mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" lspace="0em" mathcolor="#000000" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">X</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(O;Z|X)</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> between the model’s outputs and CoTs to quantify the information content in the reasoning traces.</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Monitor Accuracy</span><span id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">: The accuracy of the monitor in correctly identifying whether the model is providing a hacky answer.</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Hacking Rate</span><span id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">: The percentage of samples for which the model output passes the task verifier, but not the true verifier.</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">True Pass Rate</span><span id="S5.I1.i4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> / </span><span id="S5.I1.i4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Correct Answer Rate</span><span id="S5.I1.i4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">: The percentage of samples for which the model output passes the true verifier. This is a measure of true model performance.</span></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Results and Analysis</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">In Figure </span><a href="#S5.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 5.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a><span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> we show results on the MBPP and BigMath environments for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct trained under five different reward configurations. To make it easier to decipher the general trend, we plot using exponential moving average with smoothing factor of </span><math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">0.2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.2</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Mutual information reward improves CoT-monitorability:</span><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">
Figure </span><a href="#S5.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 5.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> shows the evolution of MI (</span><math id="S5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(O;Z|X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">O</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">;</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Z</mi></mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" lspace="0em" mathcolor="#000000" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">X</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(O;Z|X)</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">) during training.
Notably, mutual information deteriorates during RL training for models optimizing </span><math id="S5.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Task</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> and </span><math id="S5.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}+R_{\mathrm{Monitor}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Task</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">+</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Monitor</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}+R_{\mathrm{Monitor}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">.
This decrease in MI for </span><math id="S5.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}+R_{\mathrm{Monitor}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Task</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">+</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Monitor</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}+R_{\mathrm{Monitor}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> is accompanied by a decrease in monitor accuracy, indicating the obfuscation behavior due to optimizing against CoT monitor that was also observed by </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Baker et al. (2025)</a></cite><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.10" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">. Additionally, monitor accuracy also decreases for </span><math id="S5.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Task</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.11" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> on the BigMath environment, indicating that the monitor fails even on the natural training behavior under </span><math id="S5.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Task</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.12" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">. Inspecting completions, we observe that the agent often provides genuine CoT and then flips the sign of final answer after referencing ‘negative numbers’ or ‘the hint’. Initially, this flip happens explicitly in the CoT, while later in training the sign is often flipped implicitly between CoT and answer. The latter was also observed in </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025)</a></cite><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.15" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Critically, both our proposed approaches – oracle reward and MI reward – successfully maintain higher MI values throughout training, and maintain high monitor accuracy.
This corroborates our theoretical prediction that maximizing </span><math id="S5.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(O;Z|X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">O</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">;</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Z</mi></mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" lspace="0em" mathcolor="#000000" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">X</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(O;Z|X)</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> may be an effective strategy for preserving CoT monitorability, even when optimization pressure is applied to CoT.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Reward hacking and training against CoT-monitor:</span><span id="S5.SS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">
As shown in Figure </span><a href="#S5.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 5.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a><span id="S5.SS2.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">, the model trained against a vulnerable task reward learns to hack its reward.
Although the model trained to optimize </span><math id="S5.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}+R_{\mathrm{Monitor}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Task</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">+</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Monitor</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}+R_{\mathrm{Monitor}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.SS2.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> on MBPP initially learns to hack less in the first </span><math id="S5.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="400" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">400</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">400</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.SS2.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> steps, once it learns that it can evade the monitor by obfuscating its CoT, it reverts to hacking while simultaneously fooling the CoT monitor. Hacks consist of reasonable-looking CoT that discusses a general implementation, followed by output code snippets that hardcode the visible unit tests. On BigMath, the model initially does not hack, but hacking rate steadily increases during training as the model learns to exploit the verifier. Hacks take a similar form as for runs with </span><math id="S5.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Task</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.SS2.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> only: reasonable-looking CoT with sign flips in the final output.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">In both MBPP and BigMath, hacking rate increases more slowly with the monitor present compared to </span><math id="S5.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Task</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.SS2.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> only training runs. On MBPP, hacking rate with monitor-in-the-loop plateaus around 75%, while on BigMath the model reaches near 100% hacking rate. In contrast, adding </span><math id="S5.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Oracle}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Oracle</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Oracle}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.SS2.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> or </span><math id="S5.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.SS2.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> to the reward leads to successfully unlearning hacking behavior in MBPP, and not learning hacking behavior in BigMath. Intuitively, these terms make it difficult for the model to obfuscate its CoT, which in turn allows CoT monitoring to remain effective even though it is an optimization target. We provide model completions in Appendix </span><a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Sample Model Completions ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a><span id="S5.SS2.p5.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Additional results:</span><span id="S5.SS2.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> In Appendix </span><a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Additional Results ‣ Appendix B MBPP Environment: Additional Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a><span id="S5.SS2.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> we show similar results on three additional models for the MBPP environment, including on a DeepSeek distilled reasoning model. We also include ablations of </span><math id="S5.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.SS2.p6.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> parameters </span><math id="S5.SS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.SS2.p6.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> and </span><math id="S5.SS2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.SS2.p6.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">, an ablation on monitor prompt, effect on completion lengths, and additional analyses on the ‘alignment tax’ of our </span><math id="S5.SS2.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.SS2.p6.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> term. In Appendix </span><a href="#A3.SS1" title="C.1 Additional results ‣ Appendix C BigMath Environment: Additional Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a><span id="S5.SS2.p6.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">, we discuss additional ablations on the BigMath environment. We also provide results on one additional environment in Appendix </span><a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Reasoning Gym simple-equations Environment: Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a><span id="S5.SS2.p6.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">, to study whether </span><math id="S5.SS2.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.SS2.p6.1.10" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> can assist in scenarios potentially involving steganographic behaviors.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Limitations &amp; Future Work</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Our work has some limitations that point to important avenues for future research.
Theoretically, our analysis is framed from an information-theoretic perspective and does not address the potential computational or learning-theoretic advantages that CoT monitors may have in practice.
Specifically, CoT monitors may succeed because the information might be easier to decode from CoT than outputs </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep"><span id="S6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">(</span><a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2020</a><span id="S6.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">)</span></cite><span id="S6.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">.
Empirically, while our proposed methods do mitigate reward hacking and CoT obfuscation, they do not eliminate it entirely.
These limitations suggest that there remains room for developing more advanced training objectives to further improve CoT monitorability.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Impact statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">This work advances the science of chain-of-thought monitoring and introduces techniques to make models more monitorable. These techniques can support more effective AI oversight and improve the reliability of AI safety supervision.
As such, we expect this work to have largely positive societal consequences.</span></p>
</div>
</section>

<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Appendix Contents</h2>
