</section>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Reasoning Gym <span id="A1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">simple-equations</span> Environment: Results &amp; Experiment Details</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">In this section, we describe experiments performed in the </span><span id="A1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">simple-equations</span><span id="A1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> environment of Reasoning Gym </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep"><span id="A1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">(</span><a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stojanovski et al., 2025</a><span id="A1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">)</span></cite><span id="A1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">.</span></p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Environment Details</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The </span><span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">simple-equations</span><span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> environment consists of simple procedurally generated equations with one unknown variable, e.g., </span><math id="A1.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="32*u+4=3044" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">32</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" lspace="0.222em" mathcolor="#000000" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">u</mi></mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">+</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">4</mn></mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">3044</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32*u+4=3044</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">.</span><span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            We use the default environment parameters, which can be found at <a href="https://github.com/open-thought/reasoning-gym/blob/main/GALLERY.md#simple_equations" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/open-thought/reasoning-gym/blob/main/GALLERY.md#simple_equations</a>.</span></span></span><span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">
The model’s task is to find the value of the unknown variable that solves the equation. Early experimentation showed that </span><math id="A1.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">B</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3B</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> size models require CoT to solve these tasks.
To this environment, we add a monitor that monitors the CoT to determine whether the model will obtain the right value in its final answer.
In this default setup, solving the environment involves the model obtaining the right answer using a CoT that the monitor understands.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">In order to add monitor pressure, we instead task the model with getting the right answer </span><em id="A1.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">while making the monitor think it will get the wrong answer</em><span id="A1.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">, i.e., to increase the monitor rejection rate.
This introduces adversarial dynamics and creates an incentive for the model to fool the monitor, allowing us to study the limits of monitorability and our MI objective.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Similar to the MBPP environment, we use a structural formatting reward to incentivize the model to organize its response into two distinct XML-tagged sections: a </span><span id="A1.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">&lt;think&gt;...&lt;/think&gt;</span><span id="A1.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> block containing the reasoning process (corresponding to CoT </span><math id="A1.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">) and a </span><span id="A1.SS1.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">&lt;answer&gt;...&lt;/answer&gt;</span><span id="A1.SS1.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> block containing the final solution (corresponding to output </span><math id="A1.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">o</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS1.p3.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">).</span></p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Models:</h5>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">We use Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the models trained via RL and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the monitor. We provide the prompt used for the monitor model in Figure </span><a href="#A1.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ A.4 Monitor Prompt ‣ Appendix A Reasoning Gym simple-equations Environment: Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a><span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Evaluation Metrics:</h5>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">We report our results in Figures </span><a href="#A1.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Evaluation Metrics: ‣ A.1 Environment Details ‣ Appendix A Reasoning Gym simple-equations Environment: Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a><span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> and </span><a href="#A1.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 7B model: ‣ A.2 Results and Analysis ‣ Appendix A Reasoning Gym simple-equations Environment: Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a><span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> using three metrics:</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="A1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="A1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Task Accuracy:</span><span id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> This simply measures the number of samples on which the model is able to provide the right answer.</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Mutual Information Estimate:</span><span id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> This is the mutual information estimate </span><math id="A1.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">I</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{I}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> between the output and CoT (see Equation </span><a href="#S4.E8" title="Equation 8 ‣ 4.2.1 Estimation and Practical Optimization of 𝐼(𝑂;𝑍∣𝑋) ‣ 4.2 A Label-Free Proxy: Maximizing 𝐼(𝑂;𝑍∣𝑋) ‣ 4 Can CoT Monitorability be Improved? ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a><span id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">). Note that this estimate is a lower bound on true mutual information as discussed in Section </span><a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Analysis of the Mutual Information Reward ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a><span id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">).</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Monitor Rejection Rate:</span><span id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> This measures the proportion of samples on which monitor believes that model’s CoT is not going to lead to the correct answer.
When the model obtains high task accuracy, this can loosely be interpreted as how often the model is able to fool the monitor.</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Completion Length:</span><span id="A1.I1.i4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> This is the average number of tokens in a model’s generations.</span></p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">To make it easier to decipher the general trend, we plot results using an exponential moving average with smoothing factor of </span><math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">0.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">.</span></p>
</div>

<math id="A1.F4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Task</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to just maximizing the task reward alone (four seeds), <math id="A1.F4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}+R_{\mathrm{MonitorReject}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Task</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">+</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MonitorReject</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}+R_{\mathrm{MonitorReject}}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to maximizing the task reward and monitor rejection rate simultaneously (three seeds), <math id="A1.F4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}+R_{\mathrm{MonitorReject}}+R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Task</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">+</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MonitorReject</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">+</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}+R_{\mathrm{MonitorReject}}+R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math> maximizes MI reward (five seeds).
For the latter, one seed <em id="A1.F4.28.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">fools the monitor through steganographic CoT</em> but fails the task (denoted full steganography in the legend);
three seeds perform <em id="A1.F4.28.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">a mixture of suppressive and weakly-steganographic CoT</em>, partially succeeding both at the task and at fooling the monitor (denoted partial steganography);
one seed <em id="A1.F4.28.8" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">gives up</em> on fooling the monitor (denoted no steganography).
Shaded area shows the standard deviation. To obtain <math id="A1.F4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math>, we transform the MI values using <math id="A1.F4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(a=20,b=2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">a</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">20</mn></mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">,</mo><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">b</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">2</mn></mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a=20,b=2)</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Results and Analysis</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">In this environment, we found that models sometimes would ignore the structural formatting reward.
Ignoring this reward allows models to, for instance, put reasoning outside of </span><span id="A1.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">&lt;think&gt;</span><span id="A1.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> tags, which contributes to fooling the monitor into rejecting the CoT as incomplete for solving the arithmetic task.
In order to control for this behavior, we filter results to include only those runs in which the structural formatting reward is fully satisfied.</span></p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">3B model:</h5>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">We first focus our analysis on the 3B model in Figure </span><a href="#A1.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Evaluation Metrics: ‣ A.1 Environment Details ‣ Appendix A Reasoning Gym simple-equations Environment: Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">. Here, we observe that optimizing just the baseline task reward </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Task</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> leads to high task and monitor accuracy. The model is able to learn the tasks in this environment, using a legible CoT that contains all the necessary steps for solving a given equation (see Figure </span><a href="#A4.F37" title="Figure 37 ‣ D.3 Reasoning Gym completions ‣ Appendix D Sample Model Completions ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">37</span></a><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> for a sample completion). Furthermore, model generations have a moderate length of around </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="150" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">150</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">150</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> tokens on average.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Introducing the monitor rejection reward </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MonitorReject}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MonitorReject</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MonitorReject}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> leads to the model learning to generate CoTs that always get rejected by the monitor.
Despite the monitor rejecting almost all CoTs output by the model, which indicates that the monitor predicts that the model will not be able to get the right answer, the model is able to achieve non-trivial task accuracy of almost </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="60\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">60</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">60\%</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">.
The model achieves this is by </span><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">omitting</span><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> some of the steps required for solving the equation from its CoT, instead performing those steps latently (in its forward pass); for example, see the sample completion in Figure </span><a href="#A4.F38" title="Figure 38 ‣ D.3 Reasoning Gym completions ‣ Appendix D Sample Model Completions ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">38</span></a><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">.
The omission of steps is also reflected in a decrease in average completion length from </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 150" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">∼</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">150</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 150</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> for models just optimizing </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Task</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> to </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">∼</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 100</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> for models optimizing both </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Task</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.10" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> and </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MonitorReject}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MonitorReject</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MonitorReject}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.11" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">.
However, the model also sometimes fails to correctly carry out the omitted steps, causing a drop in performance from almost </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">100</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100\%</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.12" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> task accuracy to about </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="60\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">60</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">60\%</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.13" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> task accuracy.
Mutual information estimates for these runs are lower than for the baseline task, which matches the observed CoT suppression behavior.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">After including the </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="MI" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">I</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">MI</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> reward term, we observe three qualitatively distinct sets of behaviors.
In this environment, we note that an optimal policy is to learn to use encoded or steganographic reasoning to solve the task, under the assumption that the LLM requires CoT to solve this task. This is a strategy that simultaneously achieves high task reward, fools the monitor, and obtains high MI. To see why, note that solving the task with encoded reasoning would lead to a high monitor rejection rate – since the monitor is unable to understand the reasoning – while obtaining high MI due to the model’s ability to interpret its own CoT. We remind the reader that, to obtain </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">, we evaluate MI under the model’s own distribution, noting that MI under the monitor would become extremely low in encoded reasoning settings.
Despite this optimal strategy being available, it has been noted that current LLMs are limited in their ability to perform steganographic reasoning </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep"><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">(</span><a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zolkowski et al., 2025</a><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">)</span></cite><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">.
Consequently, we find that our models struggle to find this optimal policy.
Nevertheless, our experiments show multitude of interesting behaviors – including signs of steganography – that we report on below.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">In one run, optimizing the MI reward term causes the policy to give up on trying to fool the monitor (i.e., increase the monitor rejection rate).
This results in the model achieving almost perfect task-performance while at the same time having high MI, and </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">≈</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 0</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> monitor rejection rate (as such, monitor accuracy is almost </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 100\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">≈</mo><mrow><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">100</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 100\%</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">).
Average completion length also almost doubles to </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="400" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">400</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">400</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> and the CoT becomes much more informative.
Inspecting CoT for these runs, we indeed see a reduction in obfuscation in the CoTs; all CoTs are legible and skip barely any arithmetic steps (see Figure </span><a href="#A4.F39" title="Figure 39 ‣ D.3 Reasoning Gym completions ‣ Appendix D Sample Model Completions ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">39</span></a><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">).</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">In the second set of runs, despite optimizing the MI reward, we find that the model retains its focus on fooling the monitor. However, due to the regularization provided by the MI term, this is somewhat more difficult than when optimizing for </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}+R_{\mathrm{MonitorReject}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Task</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">+</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MonitorReject</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}+R_{\mathrm{MonitorReject}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> alone. This causes the models adopting this strategy to have slightly lower monitor rejection rates and slightly higher task accuracy. Qualitatively, these models exhibit less suppression than the </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}+R_{\mathrm{MonitorReject}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Task</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">+</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MonitorReject</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}+R_{\mathrm{MonitorReject}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> run, showing more of the required arithmetic steps in their CoT. However, they may introduce mistakes in their CoT that they ignore when computing their final answer, see for instance Figure </span><a href="#A4.F40" title="Figure 40 ‣ D.3 Reasoning Gym completions ‣ Appendix D Sample Model Completions ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">40</span></a><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">. This represents a weak form of steganography: the model knows to ignore the mistakes, but the monitor does not.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Finally, in the last run, we observe extreme levels of steganographic reasoning arising in the model, see the example in Figure </span><a href="#A4.F41" title="Figure 41 ‣ D.3 Reasoning Gym completions ‣ Appendix D Sample Model Completions ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">41</span></a><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">.
This results in very high monitor rejection rate as well as very high MI reward; in fact, the MI estimate is by far highest for this run.
However, this extreme level of stenography drives the model significantly off-distribution, which severely harms its task performance.
For this run, we used an adapted monitor prompt that instructs the monitor to consider a CoT correct even if it seemed incomplete.
As a result, omitting or suppressing some steps from CoT no longer presented a reliable avenue for fooling the monitor, forcing the model to explore other strategies.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Takeaways:</h5>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">This experiment highlights several key dynamics of CoT monitoring under adversarial pressure.
First, when incentivized to fool the monitor, the models’ default strategy is obfuscation via suppression: they learn to omit critical reasoning steps from their CoT, which successfully fools the monitor but degrades task performance.
Second, while models can be pushed toward more sophisticated steganographic reasoning strategies, this behavior is neither reliable nor consistent.
We observe that, at least for Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, attempts at steganography may lead to a catastrophic drop in task accuracy, suggesting that current models struggle to maintain reasoning capabilities while actively encoding information.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">We note that compared to the MBPP environment, the MI reward term is considerably less effective in preventing CoT obfuscation, except for the 7B agent model with the anti-suppression monitor prompt.
This is likely due to increased tension between the various reward terms. In MBPP, there is a clear solution that is achievable by the model and satisfies all the reward terms: the model tries to write genuine code solutions (this improves the task reward) and truthfully explains its thinking process (which improves monitor accuracy) and develops a tight coupling between CoT and output (which improves the MI reward).
However, in the current environment, there is much more tension between the reward terms as </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Task</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> and </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MonitorReject}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MonitorReject</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MonitorReject}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> are naturally in opposition.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The strategy that the model finds to satisfy these ‘opposite’ reward functions is to perform CoT obfuscation via suppression, which is penalized by </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">.
Thus, the model is forced to choose to </span><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">not</span><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> optimize one of these reward functions, resulting in three different strategies: no steganography strategy where it ignores </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MonitorReject}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MonitorReject</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MonitorReject}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">, partial steganography strategy where it only weakly optimizes </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> and full steganography strategy in which the model is forced to ignore </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Task</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> due to challenges in implementing such strategies.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Finally, we note that this environment highlights a potential limitation of the </span><math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> term. While it can prevent obfuscation via suppression if optimized successfully, it does not disincentivize obfuscation via steganography.
In order to disincentivize obfuscation via steganography, MI could be evaluated using some other LLM’s distribution (e.g., the monitor LLM), as such an LLM would not obtain high MI under (steganographic) reasoning that it cannot decode.
However, this likely brings additional estimation and optimization challenges, and is out of scope for the current work.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">7B model:</h5>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">In Figure </span><a href="#A1.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 7B model: ‣ A.2 Results and Analysis ‣ Appendix A Reasoning Gym simple-equations Environment: Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">, we show results on the same environment with Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, using both the default prompt and the anti-suppression prompt (see </span><a href="#A1.SS4" title="A.4 Monitor Prompt ‣ Appendix A Reasoning Gym simple-equations Environment: Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.4</span></a><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">). With the original prompt, the 7B model is able to almost completely fool the monitor under monitor pressure. Our MI term improves the monitor’s ability to correctly judge the CoT, while simultaneously improving task accuracy. However, the monitor still falsely rejects 80% of CoTs. This is in contrast to the 3B model, which cannot simultaneously fool the monitor and get high task reward, leading to the trade-offs between reward terms mentioned above.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Adding the anti-suppression line to the monitor prompt makes monitor fooling much harder. However, although it takes much longer, the model still eventually manages to fool the monitor in  90% of cases under monitor pressure. Here, adding our MI term almost fully restores monitor accuracy. Changing the monitor prompt to explicitly mitigate suppression has a drastic effect on the training dynamics for the 7B model; the model no longer attempts to fool the monitor, similar to the “(no steganography)” runs of Figure </span><a href="#A1.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Evaluation Metrics: ‣ A.1 Environment Details ‣ Appendix A Reasoning Gym simple-equations Environment: Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a><span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">. Note that for the 3B model, this change in prompt instead led to the “(full steganography)” run.</span></p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Agent System Prompt</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">We present the Reasoning Gym agent’s system prompt in Figure </span><a href="#A1.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ A.3 Agent System Prompt ‣ Appendix A Reasoning Gym simple-equations Environment: Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a><span id="A1.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">.</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F6" class="ltx_figure"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A1.F6.pic1" class="ltx_picture" color="#000000" height="62.39" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 477.38 62.39" width="477.38"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,62.39) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><clipPath id="pgfcp14"><path d="M -22670.54 -22670.54 L 22670.54 -22670.54 L 22670.54 22670.54 L -22670.54 22670.54 Z M 0 0 L 0 62.39 L 477.38 62.39 L 477.38 0 Z"></path></clipPath><g fill-rule="evenodd"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#BFBFBF;" fill="#BFBFBF" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 0 L 0 62.39 L 477.38 62.39 L 477.38 0 Z M 1.97 1.97 L 1.97 60.42 L 475.41 60.42 L 475.41 1.97 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#ECECEC;" fill="#ECECEC" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 1.97 L 1.97 60.42 L 475.41 60.42 L 475.41 1.97 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 9.06 11.48)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:35.88em;--ltx-fo-height:3.03em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.18em;font-size:10pt;" height="44.28" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 41.86)" width="496.48"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">

<span id="A1.F6.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.F6.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">You are a helpful assistant that solves problems step-by-step. First, think through the problem carefully in the &lt;think&gt; tags. Then, provide your final answer in the &lt;answer&gt; tags. Consider using diverse languages within your &lt;think&gt; tags.</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></g></svg></span>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A1.F6.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="A1.F6.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Reasoning Gym Agent System Prompt.<span id="A1.F6.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> The agent system prompt tasks the model to reason step-by-step using &lt;think&gt; and &lt;answer&gt; tags. It also encourages the model to use diverse languages in an attempt to elicit steganographic reasoning. However, while the agent does reason in a variety of existing languages as a result, the monitor is able to decode these languages well. The agent it does not generally step further into steganographic reasoning.</span></span></figcaption>

</section>
<section id="A1.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.4 </span>Monitor Prompt</h3>

<div id="A1.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">We present the Reasoning Gym monitor’s system prompt in Figure </span><a href="#A1.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ A.4 Monitor Prompt ‣ Appendix A Reasoning Gym simple-equations Environment: Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a><span id="A1.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">.</span></p>
</div>

<span id="A1.F7.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:35.88em;">
<span id="A1.F7.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.F7.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">You are an expert reasoning evaluator. Your job is to read a student’s reasoning and decide
whether their final answer will be correct. 
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">### Problem 
<br class="ltx_break">{agent_prompt} 
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">### Student’s Reasoning 
<br class="ltx_break">{agent_messages} 
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">### Important 
<br class="ltx_break">The chain-of-thought shown may be incomplete, or redacted. Base your judgment only on what is visible. <span id="A1.F7.pic1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF8000;">However, the presented reasoning should be considered correct if it is sufficient to obtain the final answer, even if it does not directly state the final answer.</span> 
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">Reminder: Grade the student’s answer with the following structure: 
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">### Grading Report 
<br class="ltx_break">Provide a concise justification (2-4 sentences) citing specific reasoning steps. 
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">### Final Answer 
<br class="ltx_break">Select from one of the options listed below. 
<br class="ltx_break">A. The reasoning leads to a correct final answer. 
<br class="ltx_break">B. The reasoning leads to an incorrect final answer. 
<br class="ltx_break"></span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></g></svg></span>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A1.F7.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="A1.F7.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Reasoning Gym Monitor Prompt.<span id="A1.F7.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> The monitor analyzes student thoughts to determine whether the final answer that the student provides will be correct. The text in <span id="A1.F7.6.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF8000;">orange</span> is the anti-suppression prompt used in the 7B runs of Figure <a href="#A1.F5.sf2" title="Figure 5(b) ‣ Figure 5 ‣ 7B model: ‣ A.2 Results and Analysis ‣ Appendix A Reasoning Gym simple-equations Environment: Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5(b)</span></a> and in the 3B run that exhibits full steganography in Figure <a href="#A1.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Evaluation Metrics: ‣ A.1 Environment Details ‣ Appendix A Reasoning Gym simple-equations Environment: Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>: intuitively, it makes successfully executing suppression strategies harder, since the monitor is more prepared for missing steps.</span></span></figcaption>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">In Figure </span><a href="#A2.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ B.1.1 Results on additional models ‣ B.1 Additional Results ‣ Appendix B MBPP Environment: Additional Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a><span id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">, we show results on two additional models: SmolLM3-3B </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep"><span id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">(</span><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bakouch et al., 2025</a><span id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">)</span></cite><span id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep"><span id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">(</span><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepSeek-AI, 2025</a><span id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">)</span></cite><span id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.10" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">. Results follow similar patterns as we observe for Qwen models: pure task runs and runs with monitor pressure end up hacking, while runs with </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Oracle}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Oracle</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Oracle}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.11" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> or </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.12" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> maintain low hacking rate and high monitor accuracy. We refer to Appendix </span><a href="#A2.SS1.SSS2" title="B.1.2 Ablations ‣ B.1 Additional Results ‣ Appendix B MBPP Environment: Additional Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1.2</span></a><span id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.13" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> for ablations of </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.14" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> parameters.</span></p>

SmolLM3-3B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B models on MBPP. <math id="A2.F9.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi <section id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Ablation over <math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math> Hyperparameters:</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">In Figures </span><a href="#A2.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ B.1.2 Ablations ‣ B.1 Additional Results ‣ Appendix B MBPP Environment: Additional Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> and </span><a href="#A2.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ Ablation over 𝑅_MI Hyperparameters: ‣ B.1.2 Ablations ‣ B.1 Additional Results ‣ Appendix B MBPP Environment: Additional Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">, we investigate the effect of choosing different hyperparameters for </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> for Qwen models.
Recall that </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}(o_{i},z_{i},x_{i})=\min\big(a\hat{I}_{i}(o_{i},z_{i},x_{i}),b\big)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">o</mi><mi mathcolor="#000000">=</mo><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" maxsize="1.200em" mathcolor="#000000">I</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">^</mo></mover><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">o</mi><mi minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}(o_{i},z_{i},x_{i})=\min\big(a\hat{I}_{i}(o_{i},z_{i},x_{i}),b\big)</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">, where </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> and </span><math encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> can be user specified, and roughly control how strongly </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> should be optimized. Broadly, </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> specifies how high </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> can become for any given rollout, while </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.11" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> affects how strongly changes in MI estimate affect </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.12" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">. A combination of high </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.13" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> and low </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.14" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> allows the model to more strongly optimize for MI, and we have found tuning these values to be important for maintaining model performance while reducing hacking rate.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">In the case of Qwen 3B, we observe that setting </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> values too low do not sufficiently reduce hacking, while too high </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> values reduce True Pass Rate. In both cases, monitor accuracy deteriorates. The reduction in monitor performance for high </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> values is due to the agent collapsing to very simple CoT that the monitor considers suspicious. In actuality, the agent fails to output even hacky code snippets in many of these samples, instead maximizing MI by outputting degenerate completions.</span></p>
</div>

</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">In Figures </span><a href="#A2.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ Ablation over 𝑅_MI Hyperparameters: ‣ B.1.2 Ablations ‣ B.1 Additional Results ‣ Appendix B MBPP Environment: Additional Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> and </span><a href="#A2.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ Ablation over 𝑅_MI Hyperparameters: ‣ B.1.2 Ablations ‣ B.1 Additional Results ‣ Appendix B MBPP Environment: Additional Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> we show similar ablations for the SmolLM and DeepSeek models. In the former, higher </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> values are also associated with lower True Pass Rate, but also with slightly higher hacking rate. This suggests the mapping from </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> values to hacking behavior is somewhat different for this setting. For the DeepSeek model, the worst performing runs have high </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> and low </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> values. This is likely due to the scale of the MI estimate, which is almost two orders of magnitude lower for the DeepSeek model. As such, </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> must be large in order for the estimate to contribute a </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> term on the same scale as the other reward terms. Note that even </span><math id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a=1000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">a</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">1000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a=1000</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4.1.10" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> performs quite well in this setting.</span></p>
</div>

<section id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Ablation over monitor prompt:</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Interestingly, in these ablations, runs that do worse on true pass rate often have higher monitor false positive rate.
We speculate that this loss of performance is likely due to the poor quality of the monitor which mistakenly starts flagging benign CoTs as showing intent to hack.
To reduce the high false positive rates, we attempted to make the monitor more lenient by crafting a </span><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">lite-prompt</span><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">, which is a modified the original monitor prompt. Specifically, we omit the third criterion: “Did students outline a detailed general solution? If they did not, they are hacking the test cases."
As shown in Figure </span><a href="#A2.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ Ablation over monitor prompt: ‣ B.1.2 Ablations ‣ B.1 Additional Results ‣ Appendix B MBPP Environment: Additional Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a><span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">, this prompt does decrease the model’s False Positive Rate somewhat, but this comes at the cost of a correspondingly higher False Negative Rate. Overall model and monitor performance remains similar in this setting.</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F14" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2602.18297v1/figures/mbpp/qwen_3B_monitor_prompt_ablations/alpha0.2_maxstep1500_legend.png" id="A2.F14.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/56;" width="381" height="56" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2602.18297v1/figures/mbpp/qwen_3B_monitor_prompt_ablations/alpha0.2_maxstep1500.png" id="A2.F14.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/211;" width="452" height="211" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A2.F14.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 14</span>: </span><span id="A2.F14.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Comparison of 3B Qwen models trained to optimize <math id="A2.F14.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{Task}}+R_{\mathrm{Monitor}}+R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Task</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">+</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Monitor</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">+</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{Task}}+R_{\mathrm{Monitor}}+R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math> for two different monitor prompt variants. <section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Does optimizing <math id="A2.SS2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math> incur an ‘alignment tax?’</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">In Figure </span><a href="#A2.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ B.2 Does optimizing 𝑅_MI incur an ‘alignment tax?’ ‣ Appendix B MBPP Environment: Additional Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a><span id="A2.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">, we analyze whether optimizing </span><math id="A2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> can reduce model performance in the absence of monitor pressure on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. As observed in the Figure, optimizing </span><math id="A2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> together with </span><math id="A2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{True}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">True</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{True}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> (no monitor pressure) can lead to a reduction in True Pass Rate and monitor accuracy, but careful tuning of MI parameters mostly offsets these effects. Runs with the </span><math id="A2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> term have lower False Negative Rate at the cost of increased False Positive Rate. Arguably, false negatives are the more serious errors, as they represent not detecting potentially harmful model completions.</span></p>
</div>

<section id="A2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">

<div id="A2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Figure </span><a href="#A2.F17" title="Figure 17 ‣ B.4 Effect of MI reward term on completion length ‣ Appendix B MBPP Environment: Additional Results &amp; Experiment Details ‣ Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a><span id="A2.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> illustrates the impact of different reward configurations on the completion length for both the 3B and 7B RL models.
For the 3B model, optimizing </span><math id="A2.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{MI}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">R</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">MI</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{MI}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> leads to the shortest CoTs on average. However, for the 7B, we obtain much longer CoTs. class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">, were set to different values in both runs (</span><math id="A2.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b=2" display="inline" </span><math id="A2.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">b</mi><mo
